list.listitem: A neck mass in an adult should be considered cancer until ruled out. C
Initial evaluation of a neck mass begins with the determination of whether it is congenital, infectious/inflammatory, or possibly neoplastic ( and ). C
If neoplasm is suspected, or infection/inflammation is suspected but there is no response to antibiotics, image it with CT or MRI and refer for probable fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy. C
Referral to otolaryngologist should be entertained early. C

background.definition: Palpable mass in the neck that may be congenital, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic.

list.listitem: The National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey estimated over 100,000 visits to family physicians for "swelling, mass or lump in head or neck", approximately .07% of all visits in 2000.
Broadly, causes include malignant neoplasm, benign neoplasm, a congenital lesion, an infectious process, or an inflammatory process.
See Differential Diagnosis table for a detailed review of causes of neck mass.

Individuals younger than 40 years of age are overwhelmingly diagnosed with benign processes such as congenital and inflammatory lesions, while individuals older than 40 years of age should be considered to have cancer until proven otherwise. Male gender and alcohol use are also risk factors for malignancy.
Varies widely by etiology.
Adult neck mass is considered malignant until proven otherwise. C
Imaging should be obtained for suspicious masses, large masses, or those not responsive to therapy (CT, MRI, or U/S). C
FNA is the test of choice for pathological diagnosis in almost all cases. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually a metastatic deposit in a cervical lymph node
Often found in submandibular triangle or in tail of parotid
Often a single large mass or multiple small neck masses
Painless growing mass, discrete mass in an otherwise normal appearing gland. Biopsy to diagnose
Usually show up in first 10 years of life, contain mucous or pus-like fluid, and are midline of the neck
Soft lump or draining opening on one side of the neck, very common first decade of life,
Small, nonpainful lump beneath the skin. Grayish-white, cheesy, foul-smelling material may drain from the cyst
Typically acute onset; may remain chronically enlarged
Hemoptysis, unintended weight loss, fever, night sweats, pleurisy
Scaly rash, red bumps, fever, soreness of eyes
Lymphadenopathy and erythematous, tender pustules or papules at inoculation site
Mouth pain and swelling, presence of calculi

list.listitem: American Academy of Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery (AAOHNS) guidelines (2017) recommend further evaluation of any patient with characteristics that could recommend malignancy: present more than 2 weeks with no fluctuance or infectious characteristics. High risk characteristics include fixation to adjacent tissues, firm consistency, size >1.5 cm, or ulceration of overlying skin.
Obtain a history of the duration, growth pattern, tobacco and alcohol use, and any symptoms (eg, pain, dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, stridor, otalgia, weight loss, fever, chills).

Perform a complete head and neck examination, including inspection of all mucosal surfaces, concentrating on the location, mobility, and consistency of the mass. Hard or fixed masses are suspicious for malignancy.

Neck masses can be present anywhere, and location of the mass is important for determining the diagnosis. Masses that arise quickly (ie, hours to days) usually are benign and often inflammatory, while those that arise with slow growth are more commonly neoplastic. Neck masses observed in young children may be congenital.
Pain should arouse suspicion, but can occur with infectious/inflammatory masses as well as neoplastic processes.
Otalgia, dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness indicate involvement of the upper aerodigestive tract.

Decision to perform imaging should be made on a case by case basis; however, most adult patients with masses suspicious for malignancy, those with large masses impinging on other structures, or those with masses unresponsive to medical treatment (ie, antibiotics) will require imaging.
Ultrasound is an excellent test for suspected thyroid masses.
Ultrasound is often effective for determining the need for surgical referral in pediatric midline neck masses.
Contrast enhanced CT and MRI are recommendeed by AAOHNS guidelines for evaluation of neck masses suspected of being malignant.
Consider 18F-FDG PET-CT to further evaluate FNA result of cancer with unknown primary.

Though very few diagnoses can be made with imaging alone (ie, carotid body tumors), imaging provides important information as to location, size, and relationship to surrounding structures; and therefore often impacts on the diagnostic approach or treatment path chosen.
Fine needle aspiration (FNA) of solitary neck masses has become a well-accepted, safe, and cost-effective procedure in the diagnosis of neck masses.

It is recommended by AAOHNS guidelines (2017) as the initial test when malignancy is suspected. Patients with a cystic neck mass, as determined by FNA or imaging studies, should undergo further evaluation until a diagnosis is obtained and it should not be assumed that the mass is benign.
Ultrasound-guided needle biopsy: Indicated when mass is not easily palpable, or when previous FNA has been nondiagnostic.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the adult patient with a neck mass or pediatric patient with a neck mass of suspected non-congenital origin.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the pediatric patient with a suspected congenital neck mass.
See separate chapters for evaluation of thyroid nodule, thyroglossal duct cyst, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and cat scratch disease.

cell.label: Neck mass: congenital mass suspected (eg, presents in child, midline, and/or at anterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle)?
CT scan or MRI. Lesion requires biopsy?
Refer for FNA biopsy (preferred) or excisional biopsy.
Observation. Lesion persists or increases in size at 4-6-wk follow-up?
Observe lesion and have patient return if it changes in appearance or recurs.
Refer to specialist for evaluation and treatment based on workup and staging.
Infectious or inflammatory mass (eg, acute onset, pain, or upper respiratory infection present)?
Treat with broad-spectrum antibiotics for 2-3 wk.
Suspect neoplastic, especially if slow growth in adult. CT scan or MRI. Lesion requires biopsy?
Refer for FNA biopsy (preferred) or excisional biopsy.
